catalog_quote: Eichner (1986a and 1986b) has convincingly established the essentials of the Lydian accent. While certain details of his analysis may require revision, the skepticism of Gusmani (1988b and elsewhere) of the overall scheme is wholly unjustified. As Eichner demonstrates, the Lydian vowels /e/, /o/, /ã/, and /ẽ/ regularly occur only under the accent. Using this and other evidence (syncope and meter), he concludes that all simplex Lydian words are marked by a single accent, which is free to appear on any syllable. Aside from obscure and unanalyzable sequences, the only exceptions to this rule are univerbations of preverb and verb, and indeed, virtually all cases involve specifically the preverbs ẽn- and ẽt- “in(to).” Since metrical evidence suggests that in preverb–verb combinations the accent falls on the verb, the irregular appearance of ẽ in these cases is probably due to the influence o…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the page scan we hold of Melchert 2004, sec. 3.3, pp.604-605, exactly at the stated locator (read visually from and). (2) Deciding source: an authoritative 2004 encyclopedia grammar sketch by Melchert summarizing Eichner 1986a/b; extinct corpus language, so 'stress' is a philological reconstruction and no instrumental study can exist. Three held open specialist sources from 2023-2026 (Kloekhorst, Yakubovich, Billing) restate the same free, lexically/formationally determined accent with the same diagnostics; nothing seen suggests a fixed or weight-computed position. (3) Better/fuller sources exist but are print or paywalled (Eichner 1986a, 1987; Gérard 2005; Melchert 1994) or author-distributed only (Billing 2025 diss.); open-access probes today all failed (DiVA refused/timeout, Brill captcha, OAPEN none, NINO BiOr

sources.note: First-hand word-prosodic typology of the Luwic languages on Hyman's (2009) stress-accent / pitch accent / tone continuum: Lydian satisfies obligatoriness and culminativity (one accent per word, after Eichner 1986/1987), has non-demarcative accent location, more vowel oppositions (a e i o u a~ e~ vs a i u) and vowel lengthening (aa) in accented syllables, and widespread syncope/apocope in unaccented ones; conclusion: every Luwic language fits a stress-accent profile and Proto-Luwic (and Proto-Anatolian) is reconstructed with stress accent - i.e. no lexical tone or pitch accent is posited for L…
